source.title: Emergent Symbol-like Number Variables in Artificial Neural Networks
source.authors: Satchel Grant; Noah D. Goodman; James L. McClelland

record.tranche_reason: The study measures causal alignment of numeric task variables in toy neural networks, not sparse-feature superposition, capacity competition, SAE features, or feature overlap. Its dimensionality analyses concern learned numeric variables in this different setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for causally intervening on numeric variables represented in neural activity. These bear on neural representations generally, but do not test the claim versions about sparse features or their superposition. The one-dimensional results use a learned invertible linear alignment and do not establish that the model's native features are one-dimensional directions. Width-related IIA results and other larger-subspace alignments are not recorded as claim-version results.
record.test_reason: The study aligns task variables (Count, Phase) in small RNNs/transformers to symbolic algorithms via DAS. It does not test sparse-feature superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE features in LLMs, or whether superposed features are 1-D. It cites Toy Models of Superposition only as support for distributed coding. Its observation that raw neurons contribute to both Phase and Count is a related distributed-coding finding, not a superposition test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also conclude that shallow transformers use anti-Markovian, recompute-from-context solutions, and prove this is necessary without enough attention layers. They add that DAS IIA rises with GRU hidden size, which they speculatively attribute to more orthogonal subspaces.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains GRUs, LSTMs, and small Transformers on numeric-equivalence tasks and analyzes causal alignments with symbolic algorithms; it does not use the sparse-feature superposition toy-model setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported alignment outcomes vary with architecture, task variant, alignment function (orthogonal versus linear), and intervention subspace size.

fits_no_version.finding: 1-D linear alignment coordinates support causal interchange of Count/Phase/Up-Up variables with IIA 0.51–0.95 depending on architecture, task and variable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Numeric task variables in small RNNs can be causally manipulated via 1-D learned linear subspaces, with accuracy varying by task and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching two Count-correlated raw neurons (12, 18) in a 20-d LSTM gave IIA 0.399, with no consistent error pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual neurons correlated with a variable may not causally carry it; subspace interventions outperform single-neuron patching.

fits_no_version.finding: Many raw neurons play a causal role in both aligned Phase and Count activity in a 20-d LSTM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task variables are distributed across neurons, with neurons shared between variables (mixed selectivity), without a test of capacity or sparsity.

record.problems: The tasks are narrow synthetic numeric-equivalence tasks rather than sparse-feature or language-model settings. The Linear Alignment Function can recover variables through an invertible mapping, so its one-dimensional coordinates do not establish native feature dimensionality. The study reports no uncertainty estimates for the listed IIA values.
record.rows_left_out: Supplementary Table 1's larger-subspace alignments and width-related IIA results in Figure 3 are not extracted: they measure alignment to task-specific symbolic variables, not sparse-feature superposition or feature dimensionality.

untested.parts: All: sparse features exceeding dimensions, near-orthogonal overlap, sparsity transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition as cause of polysemanticity.
All: 1-D learned LAF alignments of task variables do not address dimensionality of superposed features.

record.verdict_notes: Record's T6/cites_only assessment is sound. The width-IIA result (Fig. 3b) and the authors' speculation about orthogonality at higher dimension are loosely related to superposition, but no measurement of feature interference was made.

versions.untested_parts: Sparse features exceeding dimensionality, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or gives important features dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure or evidences superposition.
Feature spread in LLMs and recovery of sparse LLM features with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.

Whether features in superposition are native one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features. The study tests one-dimensional coordinates in learned alignments of numeric task variables, not dimensions of superposed features.
